rationale: The two ontology types this lane had no verdict for. `imports` and `exports` are in the ontology, in the enum, and in the traversal default, and csharp emitted NEITHER: measured 0 of 269,352 relationships over 1,200 roslyn files carried either label, while the same files produced 8,941 `references` rows with `metadata.isImport === true` — the dependency existed and the graph had no label for it. So: (1) every `using` directive now also publishes an `imports` row, and (2) the assembly's public type surface, which the analyzer already computed into `result.exports` and published to no relationship at all, now publishes `exports` rows. Both pins below are written against decisions that are OBSERVABLE from the edge alone, because a fixture the pre-change analyzer would also have passed is not a fixture. The `importKind` pins are the reason: four import shapes share ONE grammar node (`using_directive`), and until this round the graph could not tell `using X;` from `using static X;` from `using A = X;` from `global using X;` — they were all one undifferentiated `references` row. Re-probed from the emitted rows after the change, in both directions: the four `importKind` values, the alias-metadata role, the two namespace spellings selecting the same export set, and the forbids for every shape that must NOT appear. The namespace-spelling pins exist because the first version of the exports rule reproduced a defect this lane had already fixed once: `!parentContext` cannot see a file-scoped namespace, so it exported those files' types and it also could not see a NESTED type, so `NestedPublic` was published as an assembly export. Both directions are pinned, and `NestedPublic` is pinned by name in the forbids.

expectSymbols.name: NestedPublic
expectSymbols.note: the nested type IS a symbol; it is only the EXPORT that it is not

expectImports.comment: `using static` — the grammar has no using_static_directive; the target is still a namespace-shaped name
alias form: the TARGET, never the alias
`using global::System.IO;` — the `global::` qualifier is removed, so this is the same module as the unqualified spelling
`global using static` — the rarest of the four shapes
`extern alias LegacyLib;` is an import directive with its own node type (`extern_alias_directive`) and produced NOTHING before this round — no payload row, no relationship, no references edge

expectExports.name: Acme.Surface.PublicType
expectExports.comment: block-namespace form, public: exported under the FULLY QUALIFIED name, because `PublicType` alone is not a name this assembly exports

expectExports.name: Acme.Surface.IPublicContract
expectExports.comment: an interface is an exported type exactly as a class is

expectExports.name: Acme.Surface.PublicEnum
expectExports.comment: an enum is an exported type too — the enum branch's rule is stated, not inherited by luck

expectExports.name: Acme.FileScoped.FileScopedPublic
expectExports.comment: THE PIN THAT MATTERS: the file-scoped namespace spelling selects the SAME set as the block form. The pre-fix guard could not see a file-scoped namespace at all and published 300 of 300 top-level declarations on the first 300 roslyn files (which are file-scoped-namespace files) as exports, under BARE names, including `internal` ones.

expectRelationships.note: `using static System.Math;` — a static-member import, NOT a namespace import. All four shapes share one node type, so this row is the only thing that tells them apart.
`using global::System.IO;` — the qualifier is stripped, so this is indistinguishable from `using System.IO;` on purpose
`global using` binds for the whole COMPILATION, not for this file. That is a different dependency from `using System.Threading;` and the label now says so.
an ASSEMBLY alias, not a namespace: `imports` only, never a `references` twin, because the differential's csharp truth does not derive this node
the line is the one the NAME is written on, not the declaration's first line — the doc comment sits above it
the references twin SURVIVES: it is R9's audited reference graph and relabelling it would turn every audited C# reference edge into a MISSING row on the shared, master-owned compared set
an internal type is still a member of its namespace; only the EXPORT is withheld
the nested type's unit is its enclosing type, and `contains` is where that fact lives

the nested-namespace shape: ONE spelling. `contains` publishes the namespace as `Acme.Inner` (the innermost declaration's own name, which already contains the outer one), and the export target agrees with it. The pre-fix value was `Acme.Outer.Acme.Inner.Doubled` — same type, two names in one result.

forbidRelationships.note: the ALIAS is a local binding, never the dependency — the CSD7/R1 fabrication this lane already fixed once for `references`, pinned again for `imports` because a new label is a new opportunity for it
same, on the `global using A = ...` form
a type EXPRESSION is not a module: D3 strips a generic alias's arguments off the module name, and the arguments are published separately as `references`, never welded into the import target

`internal` is by definition not visible outside the assembly. The pre-fix rule published it as an export with `visibility: "internal"` carried as metadata — i.e. it exported a type while recording that it should not have.
the same, fully qualified — a forbid has to be stated per spelling, because the two are different strings and the matcher compares exactly
an internal interface is not an export either
the enum branch's rule is stated separately, so it is pinned separately
and the file-scoped-namespace spelling of the same refusal
`file`-scoped visibility is never an assembly surface

a nested type is reachable only through its enclosing type, so it is not a member of the ASSEMBLY's surface. The first version of this rule published it — the fixture caught it, and the forbid is here so the fix cannot be undone by widening the visibility test alone.

THE SPELLING THE ANALYZER ACTUALLY PUBLISHES. Added after the `csharp/export-nested-types-too` mutant SURVIVED: it added the edge under the fully-qualified name and the two forbids above named the bare and the `Owner.Member` forms, so neither matched. A forbid has to name the exact string, and a fixture that forbids a shape the code never emits forbids nothing.
qualified spelling of the same refusal

the DOUBLED prefix, pinned as a forbid so the one-spelling rule is held in the negative direction too: a namespace declaration already writes its full name, so no outer namespace may be re-applied to it
and the third spelling this shape could produce — two of the three, so a rule that dropped a segment rather than doubling one is caught as well
a BARE name is not an export name for a namespaced type: `PublicType` is not a name this assembly exports, `Acme.Surface.PublicType` is. This forbid is the whole reason the published name changed.
the pre-existing references-side forbid, restated here so a single fixture holds both labels of one directive
